newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court to hear suit on Clinton forest plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court to hear suit on Clinton forest plan.

text.p: A federal appeals court Friday sided with a Northwest timber industry group and said a U.S. District Court here must consider the timber group's challenge to President Clinton's Northwest forest plan.

Reviving the timber industry's fight against Clinton's plan to save oldgrowth timber habitat of the northern spotted owl, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia overturned a decision of the U.S. District Court of the District of Columbia to dismiss the case.

The Appeals Court said the District Court here was not bound by an earlier decision by the U.S. District Court of western Washington state, which had rejected timber industry arguments and upheld Clinton's forest plan.

However, the court left it up to the District Court here to decide whether some of the industry's claims may be barred on the grounds they overlapped with the western Washington District Court action.

"We're finally going to get our opportunity to have the president's forest plan tested against the laws that direct the management of lands" by the Bureau of Land Management, Chris West, of the Northwest Forest Resource Council, said.
The Bureau of Land Management is one of the two federal agencies that oversee the federal forests.

The plan Clinton imposed in 1994 to try to save the old-growth timber habitat of the endangered spotted owl has fuelled challenges by loggers saying it would drastically cut timber production, and environmentalists who said it did not go far enough to protect the ancient trees that are essential for the spotted owl's survival.

Friday's ruling was on the Northwest Forest Council's suit against the Bureau of Land Management, which is part of the Interior Department. The industry group also sued the U.S. Forest Service, which is part of the Agriculture Department.
The U.S. District Court here had dismissed the suit against the BLM, contending that the issues had been heard before in western Washington in the industry group's lawsuit against the Forest Service.
But West, of the Northwest timber group, said there were distinct differences in the cases and some issues had not been heard.
